issues.legal_issue: A tax recovery officer who conducts a public auction is a revenue officer for the purpose of transmitting a sale certificate copy, and the registering officer must file that copy without treating the filing as registration of the original certificate.
material_facts: The purchasers acquired immovable properties at income-tax recovery auctions conducted by a Tax Recovery Officer.
The Tax Recovery Officer sent copies of the sale certificates to the Sub-Registrar under the applicable rule.
The Sub-Registrar did not make the requested record entry.
issues.conclusion: The Tax Recovery Officer is a revenue officer for this purpose, and the Sub-Registrar must file the copy received in Book No. 1; the Sub-Registrar need not transcribe the certificate or make other entries.
issues.legal_principle: Registration Act, 1908, section 89(4), requires a revenue officer granting a certificate of sale after a public auction to send a copy to the registering officer, who must file it in Book No. 1. Rule 21 of the Income Tax (Certificate Proceedings) Rules, 1962, makes a corresponding requirement for a Tax Recovery Officer. The term “revenue officer” is broad enough to include a Tax Recovery Officer. Filing a transmitted copy is distinct from registering the original document and does not require the registration procedures or transcription applicable to registration.

predicates.tax_recovery_auction: A public auction of immovable property was conducted to recover a tax debt.
predicates.sale_certificate_copy_transmitted: The public officer who conducted the auction sent a copy of the sale certificate to the registering officer.
predicates.registering_officer_must_file_copy_in_pu: The registering officer must file the transmitted copy in the relevant public record.

issues.definition: When a tax recovery auction results in a sale certificate copy being sent to the registering officer, the officer must file the copy in the public record.

issues.legal_issue: A purchaser at a tax recovery public auction need not register the sale certificate to perfect title, and non-registration does not invalidate the transfer of title.
material_facts: The purchasers acquired immovable properties at tax recovery public auctions and received sale certificates.
The purchasers sought to have the properties recorded in their names.
issues.conclusion: Registration of the sale certificate is not obligatory to perfect the purchasers’ title, and failure to register the certificate does not vitiate the transfer of title.
issues.legal_principle: Registration Act, 1908, section 17(2)(xii), exempts a certificate of sale issued to a purchaser of property sold by public auction by a civil court or revenue officer from compulsory registration. The Court held that a certificate issued by a Tax Recovery Officer is covered by that provision. The copy filed in Book No. 1 and the related public indices provide notice of the certificate’s principal contents to persons inspecting them.

predicates.tax_recovery_auction: A public auction of immovable property was conducted to recover a tax debt.
predicates.sale_certificate_issued: The public officer who conducted the auction issued a sale certificate to the purchaser.
predicates.purchaser_title_does_not_depend_on_certi: The purchaser’s title is not conditional on registration of the sale certificate.

issues.definition: When a sale certificate is issued following a tax recovery auction, the purchaser’s title does not depend on registering that certificate.

issues.legal_issue: The Court does not determine whether stamp duty is payable on a sale certificate issued after a tax recovery auction and leaves that question for adjudication through the applicable process when necessary.
material_facts: The auction notice did not promise an exemption from stamp duty.
The departmental manual indicated that stamp duty was payable, while the Tax Recovery Officer later referred to legal advice that no duty was payable.

The purchasers had not obtained an adjudication of the stamp-duty question, and the Court considered that the question could arise in the statutory processes for adjudication or when the certificate was presented for registration or evidence.
issues.conclusion: The Court expressed no opinion on whether stamp duty is payable and left the issue to be adjudicated in the normal course when necessary.
issues.legal_principle: Stamp Act, 1899, sections 3 and 29(f), and Schedule I, Article 18, were relevant to the ordinary allocation of stamp-duty liability, subject to a contract to the contrary. Sections 31 and 32 provide a process for seeking adjudication of the duty, with section 56 providing for reference to the High Court by the Chief Controlling Revenue Authority. Under sections 33 and 38, a document considered insufficiently stamped may be impounded and sent to the Collector; a court or authority receiving it in evidence may also have to impound it. The Court did not decide the certificate’s liability under these provisions.

predicates.tax_recovery_sale: Immovable property was sold at a public auction to recover a tax debt.
predicates.auction_terms_do_not_promise_stamp_exemp: The auction terms did not promise the purchaser that the sale certificate would be exempt from stamp duty.
predicates.stamp_duty_question_not_adjudicated: No competent authority had adjudicated whether stamp duty was payable on the sale certificate.
predicates.stamp_duty_payability_remains_open_for_a: Whether stamp duty is payable remains to be determined through the applicable process when necessary.

issues.definition: When a tax recovery sale’s terms do not promise a stamp-duty exemption and the duty question has not been adjudicated, payability remains open for determination through the applicable process.

issues.legal_issue: Whether a municipal transfer fee is payable on a property acquired at a tax recovery auction is left open, and the purchaser may contest the levy in appropriate proceedings.
material_facts: The purchasers sought mutation of the properties in municipal records.
The municipal transfer fee was described as additional stamp duty, but the Court was not given the relevant statutory provisions or their interpretation.
The Court expressed no opinion on stamp-duty liability.
issues.conclusion: The Court expressed no opinion on whether the municipal transfer fee was payable and left the purchasers free to contest the levy in other appropriate proceedings.
issues.legal_principle: The Court had no basis to decide the municipal transfer-fee question because the relevant statutory provisions and their interpretation had not been presented. It considered that payment of the fee might depend on whether stamp duty was payable, a question on which it expressed no opinion.

predicates.municipal_transfer_fee_disputed: A purchaser disputed a municipal fee sought in connection with recording a property transfer.
predicates.governing_basis_not_presented: The relevant legal provisions and their interpretation were not presented to the court.
predicates.purchaser_may_contest_fee_in_appropriate: The purchaser may contest the fee in appropriate proceedings.

issues.definition: When a purchaser disputes a municipal transfer fee and its governing legal basis has not been presented, the purchaser may contest the fee in appropriate proceedings.
